messages.content:
You are an evidence extraction specialist for PFAS treatment and remediation
research. Build a structured study evidence table before any narrative review
is written.

Extract one record per primary-study experiment, modeled scenario, or field
deployment that contributes usable evidence to the review task. A paper may
produce more than one record only when materially different matrices,
technologies, operating regimes, or endpoints would otherwise be conflated.

Review articles and perspectives may help identify terminology or primary
studies, but they must not be used as the source of a quantitative study
record. Never copy a review table as though it were a primary result.

For every populated source-dependent field:
- preserve the PFAS identity or class, matrix, starting concentration or
  loading, operating conditions, study scale, measured endpoint, value, unit,
  and material qualifiers when reported;
- attach only the field-level evidence locator identifiers that directly
  support that specific value or statement;
- use an empty string or empty array when the source does not report the
  information; do not infer or estimate it;
- do not turn the absence of information in the supplied packet into a study
  finding, quantitative result, or author-reported limitation unless the source
  explicitly states that absence;
- distinguish removal, separation, sorption, parent-compound loss,
  transformation, degradation, destruction, defluorination, mineralization,
  total organofluorine change, and toxicity change;
- classify endpoint_type from what was actually measured, not from the
  authors' preferred label. Parent loss alone is not destruction. Phase
  transfer is removal or separation, not degradation. Inorganic fluoride
  release or fluorine-balance closure can establish defluorination but cannot
  by itself establish mineralization. Use mineralization only when direct
  carbon-fate evidence such as CO2/inorganic-carbon production or a carbon
  balance is reported. Preserve a broader author term in reported_term and
  explain any mismatch in interpretation;
- do not normalize or compare values unless their units, denominators,
  matrices, PFAS scope, operating conditions, and endpoints permit it.

Only populate quantitative_findings when the source reports an actual numeric
value, inequality, approximate value, range, or explicit ND/not-detected
result. Put the number or censoring marker in value and the measurement unit in
unit. Normalize Unicode inequality signs to ASCII >= or <= and range dashes to
an ASCII hyphen while preserving the source wording in qualifiers. A unit or
order-of-magnitude scale without a number is not a quantitative finding.
Qualitative parent loss, intermediate formation, or disappearance belongs in
the endpoint interpretation or residual/byproduct statements instead.

Set value_form to exactly one of:
- exact_numeric: a bare number such as `99.7` or `1.2e-3`;
- approximate_numeric: `~` followed by a number;
- inequality: `<`, `<=`, `>`, or `>=` followed by a number;
- range: two numbers separated by `-` or `to`; or
- not_detected: exactly `ND`, `N/D`, `not detected`,
  `below detection limit`, or `below quantification limit`.

Put uncertainty, denominators, fold-change wording, and explanatory text in
qualifiers rather than value. A deterministic validator will remove malformed
quantitative fields before source verification.

For limitations, use basis=author_reported only when the source states the
limitation. Use basis=design_inferred only for a constraint that follows
directly from cited design evidence, such as one matrix, one compound, or
bench-scale operation. Never label missing information in the supplied packet
as a scientific limitation of the study.

Mark each record as comparable with conditions, descriptive only, or not
comparable. Comparability is an analyst inference rather than a quotation:
attach locators for the matrix, scale, conditions, endpoint, and denominator
on which the inference rests, and explain the reason. Do not reward a study
for reporting a larger percentage when its endpoint or conditions differ.

The task was derived from a defining review that is held out from all
candidate retrieval systems. The supplied anchor identifiers are an exclusion
list, not evidence. Do not extract from the anchor, cite it, reconstruct its
conclusions, or use its tables.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied evidence-table schema exactly.
Do not write the narrative review in this step.

records.citation: Pinkard, B.R.; Shetty, S.; Stritzinger, D.; Bellona, C.; Novosselov, I.V. Destruction of perfluorooctanesulfonate (PFOS) in a batch supercritical water oxidation reactor. Chemosphere 2021, 279, 130834.

comparability.reason: The study reports PFOS parent loss ("destruction"/conversion) and defluorination efficiencies as percentages under well-specified SCWO operating conditions (temperature, residence time, pressure). These endpoints and denominators (initial PFOS and total fluorine) are standard for PFAS treatment performance and, with attention to batch SCWO configuration and aqueous feed, can be compared conditionally with other PFAS destruction studies using similar percentage-based metrics.

endpoints.interpretation: Loss of PFOS parent compound in the liquid phase was quantified and reported as percent destruction/conversion versus temperature and residence time, with maximum 70.0% PFOS destruction at 500 °C after 60 min.
endpoints.reported_term: PFOS destruction, PFOS conversion, extent of destruction

endpoints.interpretation: Inorganic fluoride production from PFOS was measured and expressed as defluorination efficiency (percent fluorine conversion), with a maximum of 78.2% at 500 °C after 60 min; fluorine mass balance across reagents and products was also evaluated.
endpoints.reported_term: defluorination efficiency, fluoride production, fluorine conversion

endpoints.interpretation: Total fluorine recovery was calculated as a mass balance from initial PFOS to measured fluoride and organofluorine species. Mass balance was >75% at 475 and 500 °C, but not well closed at 425 and 450 °C, indicating an unidentified organofluorine fraction, likely including gaseous fluorinated species.
endpoints.reported_term: total fluorine mass balance, fluorine mass balance from reagents to products

endpoints.interpretation: Targeted LC-QToF-MS analysis of liquid products did not indicate production of intermediate fluorocarbons such as additional perfluoroalkane sulfonates, perfluoroalkanoic acids, or fluorotelomer sulfonates/alkanoic acids beyond PFOS, PFHpS, and PFHxS (in decreasing levels), implying either rapid further transformation or formation of undetected lower-molecular-weight fluorinated species, especially at lower temperatures where fluorine mass balance was poor.

Authors use the term 'destruction' to describe PFOS conversion and defluorination in SCWO, but direct mineralization endpoints (e.g., CO2 production, carbon balance) were not reported, so 'destruction' corresponds primarily to parent loss and defluorination rather than confirmed full mineralization.
endpoints.reported_term: destruction efficiency, efficacy for PFAS destruction

limitations.statement: Gaseous products were not analyzed; authors cite difficulty of performing non-targeted analysis of fluorocarbons in the gaseous phase at low concentrations via GC-MS, which limits identification of volatile fluorinated byproducts and contributes to poor fluorine mass balance at lower temperatures.

Fluorine mass balance was not well closed for experiments at 425 and 450 °C, suggesting formation of lower molecular weight fluorinated species in gaseous and/or liquid phases that were not captured in targeted analyses.

Transformation products were assessed only by targeted LC-QToF-MS for a defined set of perfluoroalkane sulfonates, perfluoroalkanoic acids, and fluorotelomer species, so unidentified organofluorine intermediates could remain undetected.

Experiments were conducted in a bench-scale batch SCWO reactor on PFOS-containing feed under specific temperature (425-500 °C), pressure (~25 MPa), and residence time (0-60 min) conditions, which may limit direct extrapolation to other PFAS, matrices, or continuous-flow systems.

quantitative_findings.name: Maximum PFOS destruction efficiency at 500 °C, 60 min
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: Described as maximum PFOS destruction efficiency achieved after 60 min of reaction at 500 °C in batch SCWO; also described as PFOS conversion at that condition.

quantitative_findings.name: Maximum defluorination (fluorine conversion) at 500 °C, 60 min
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: Described as maximum fluorine conversion (defluorination efficiency) achieved after 60 min of reaction at 500 °C in batch SCWO.

quantitative_findings.name: Total fluorine recovery (fluorine mass balance) at 475 and 500 °C
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: Total fluorine mass balance from reagents to products reported as >75% for experiments conducted at 475 and 500 °C; noted that fluorine mass balance is not well-closed at 425 and 450 °C.

quantitative_findings.name: Fluoride mass balance closure at 475 and 500 °C
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: Authors describe ~100% fluoride mass balance at 475 and 500 °C, supporting interpretation that C–S cleavage and subsequent C–C bond cleavage lead primarily to fluoride formation under these conditions.

quantitative_findings.name: PFOS destruction insufficiency relative to EPA HA level
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: Authors state that the maximum PFOS destruction efficiency of 70.0% achieved after 60 min of reaction at 500 °C is not sufficient to lower the resulting PFOS concentration below the EPA health advisory level of 70 ng/L; initial PFOS concentration not reported in provided text.

residuals_byproducts.statement: Targeted LC-QToF-MS analysis of liquid products did not indicate production of intermediate fluorocarbons; no perfluoroalkane sulfonates aside from PFOS, PFHpS, and PFHxS (all in decreasing levels) or perfluoroalkanoic acids were detected as reaction intermediates.

Authors attribute poor fluorine mass balance at 425 and 450 °C to potential formation of lower molecular weight fluorinated reaction products in the gaseous and/or liquid phases, which were not detected in the analyses performed.

At higher temperatures (475 and 500 °C), fluoride production increased with residence time, and near-complete fluoride mass balance (~100%) suggests extensive conversion of organofluorine to inorganic fluoride under those conditions, with limited residual unidentified fluorinated products.
